title: Alexander conquers the Levantine coast
summary: Alexander’s campaign moved through the eastern Mediterranean coast in 332 BCE, including the sieges of Tyre and Gaza before Egypt.
historicalNote: The campaign sequence is well attested in ancient histories. The atlas does not infer an otherwise unattested visit to Jerusalem as a securely historical event.

title: Alexander founds Alexandria
summary: Alexander entered Egypt in 332 BCE and founded Alexandria in 331 BCE in conventional chronology.
historicalNote: The foundation is historical; the later city developed substantially under the Ptolemies.

title: Judea in the Ptolemaic sphere
summary: After the Successor struggles, Judea formed part of the Ptolemaic-controlled southern Levant for much of the third century BCE.
historicalNote: Control shifted during the Successor wars. The atlas uses a generalized 301–200 BCE context lens rather than pretending every locality had an unchanged administrative status.

dating.label: Third century BCE; broadly 301–200 BCE for sustained Ptolemaic control

title: Greek Torah / Septuagint translation context
summary: The Greek translation of the Torah emerged in Hellenistic Egypt, conventionally associated with Alexandria in the third century BCE.
historicalNote: The translation itself is historical, but the famous seventy-two-translators court story is a later idealized tradition and should not be mapped as a literal one-day event.

dating.label: Third century BCE; exact stages debated

title: Battle of Panium and Seleucid takeover
summary: Antiochus III defeated Ptolemaic forces near Panium around 200 BCE, shifting Coele-Syria and Judea into the Seleucid sphere.
historicalNote: The battle is historical; Judea’s administrative transition is modeled as a regional process rather than an instantaneous modern border switch.

title: Seleucid temple-administration context under Seleucus IV
summary: Inscriptional evidence from the reign of Seleucus IV illuminates royal administrative involvement in temple finances across Coele-Syria/Phoenicia.
historicalNote: The inscriptional evidence is independent context. It is not treated as direct proof of the miraculous confrontation narrated in 2 Maccabees 3.

title: Antiochus IV and the Jerusalem crisis
summary: Ancient Jewish sources describe severe intervention in Jerusalem, plundering, cultic disruption and decrees restricting traditional practices under Antiochus IV.
historicalNote: The broad crisis is historically central, but 1 and 2 Maccabees differ in emphasis and sequence. The Acra’s exact footprint remains disputed.

title: Maccabean revolt begins at Modein
summary: 1 Maccabees locates the outbreak of armed resistance at Modein under Mattathias, conventionally around 167 BCE.
historicalNote: The revolt is historical, but Modein’s exact archaeological identification remains debated, so the event has no fake precise origin pin.

title: Battle of Emmaus
summary: Judas Maccabeus defeated a Seleucid force in the Emmaus region, conventionally dated to 165 BCE.
historicalNote: The settlement identification is strong; troop movements and battlefield extent are reconstructed from the literary narrative rather than excavated lines.

title: Rededication of the Jerusalem temple
summary: Judas and his supporters rededicated the temple after recapturing Jerusalem, remembered in the festival of Hanukkah.
historicalNote: The event is strongly attested in ancient Jewish literary sources. No exact excavated altar surface is identified as the rededication point.

title: Battle of Beth-zechariah
summary: A Seleucid army under Antiochus V’s government defeated Judas’s forces near Beth-zechariah; 1 Maccabees famously associates the battle with war elephants.
historicalNote: The battle is literary-historically attested; the modern site anchor is only a candidate-area location.

title: Defeat of Nicanor near Adasa
summary: Judas Maccabeus defeated Nicanor in a battle near Adasa, conventionally dated to 161 BCE.
historicalNote: Adasa remains unpinned because no modern identification is secure enough for normal map precision.

title: Death of Judas at Elasa
summary: Judas Maccabeus was killed fighting Bacchides at Elasa.
historicalNote: The historical sequence is accepted from ancient literary evidence, while Elasa’s exact location is unresolved.

title: Jonathan becomes high priest
summary: Jonathan Apphus received the high priesthood amid Seleucid dynastic competition.
historicalNote: The episode illustrates how local Judean leadership became entangled with Seleucid rival claimants.

title: Simon and effective Judean independence
summary: Under Simon, tribute obligations were remitted and Judean rule became effectively independent from Seleucid control; the Acra garrison was removed shortly afterward.
historicalNote: Ancient chronology distinguishes political concessions from the later evacuation of the Acra; the atlas avoids collapsing all milestones into one day.

title: Hasmonean incorporation of Idumea
summary: Josephus associates John Hyrcanus with the conquest/incorporation of Idumean centers including Adora and Marisa and with compulsory adoption of Judean customs.
historicalNote: The political incorporation is historical, but Josephus’s description of identity/circumcision policy is a later literary account and should not be turned into a simplistic ethnic map.

title: Destruction of the Mount Gerizim sanctuary under John Hyrcanus
summary: Josephus credits John Hyrcanus with destroying the Samaritan sanctuary on Mount Gerizim; archaeology documents a major Hellenistic sanctuary and destruction/transition.
historicalNote: The correlation between archaeological destruction and Josephus’s Hasmonean chronology is strong but interpretive rather than an inscribed “John Hyrcanus destroyed this” label.

title: Hasmonean kingship under Aristobulus I
summary: Aristobulus I is commonly treated as the first Hasmonean ruler to assume the royal title after generations of priestly leadership.
historicalNote: Josephus is the principal narrative source; titulature and chronology are reconstructed from literary and numismatic evidence.

title: Alexander Jannaeus expands the Hasmonean kingdom
summary: Alexander Jannaeus pursued extensive campaigns along the coast and in Transjordan while ruling as king and high priest.
historicalNote: Territorial extent changed repeatedly during his reign; context polygons are broad snapshots, not one permanent border.

title: Reign of Salome Alexandra
summary: Salome Alexandra ruled the Hasmonean kingdom after Alexander Jannaeus and before the civil war between Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II.

title: Hasmonean civil war
summary: Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II contested the throne, drawing in Nabataean and then Roman power.
historicalNote: This conflict is the immediate political context for Pompey’s intervention; campaign lines are reconstructed from narrative sequence.

title: Pompey captures Jerusalem
summary: Pompey intervened in the Hasmonean conflict and captured Jerusalem after a siege in 63 BCE, ending independent Hasmonean kingship.
historicalNote: The capture is well anchored historically. Detailed siege topography is described by later sources and should not be overdrawn as a centimeter-accurate battle map.

title: Roman provincial reorganization in Syria
summary: Pompey reorganized former Seleucid territories into Roman Syria, fundamentally changing the political environment around Judea.

title: Caesar, Hyrcanus II, and Antipater
summary: After the Alexandrian War, Julius Caesar confirmed arrangements that strengthened Hyrcanus II and Antipater within the Roman political order.
historicalNote: Josephus preserves decrees and narrative traditions; modern scholarship debates the textual transmission of some documentary material.

title: Parthian intervention and Antigonus II
summary: Parthian intervention in 40 BCE enabled Antigonus II Mattathias to seize power in Judea while Herod fled and sought Roman support.

title: Rome appoints Herod king
summary: The Roman Senate recognized Herod as king in 40 BCE, although he still had to conquer the kingdom militarily.
historicalNote: Roman appointment and effective possession are separated: Herod did not control Jerusalem until 37 BCE.

title: Herod captures Jerusalem
summary: With Roman support, Herod captured Jerusalem in 37 BCE and Antigonus II was removed, beginning effective Herodian rule.

title: Battle of Actium
summary: Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium, transforming the eastern Mediterranean patronage system on which Herod had depended.
historicalNote: Actium is external Roman history but crucial for understanding Herod’s political realignment.

title: Herod meets Octavian after Actium
summary: Josephus describes Herod meeting Octavian on Rhodes and successfully retaining his kingship after Antony’s defeat.
historicalNote: The meeting is known from Josephus; its exact venue and speech details are not independently recoverable.

title: Herod begins major Temple Mount expansion
summary: Herod launched a major rebuilding and enlargement of the Jerusalem temple complex, conventionally dated to 20/19 BCE.
historicalNote: The Herodian expansion is archaeologically visible in the platform and retaining walls, but reconstructions of the sanctuary superstructure remain interpretive.

title: Herod’s Caesarea and harbor mature
summary: Herod’s Caesarea Maritima and its artificial harbor became a major royal and Roman-oriented city on the coast.
historicalNote: Ancient sources and archaeology agree on the monumental program; exact dedication chronology is expressed as a range.

title: Qumran settlement and manuscript-cave context
summary: Khirbet Qumran flourished in the late Second Temple period near caves containing a diverse manuscript corpus now known as the Dead Sea Scrolls.
historicalNote: The site, caves and manuscripts are archaeological facts; identifying every manuscript with the settlement’s residents or naming the community with certainty goes beyond the evidence.

dating.label: Late second/first centuries BCE into the first century CE; phases debated

title: Jewish temple at Leontopolis in Egypt
summary: Josephus describes a Jewish temple in Egypt associated with Onias, providing an important example of Second Temple-period Jewish diversity outside Jerusalem.
historicalNote: Josephus’s Onias identifications and chronology are debated. The atlas therefore maps a candidate region rather than a recovered temple footprint.

dating.label: Second century BCE; foundation chronology debated
